title: Length Contraction
lead: Observers who measure different elapsed times for the same process still agree on their relative speed, so they must measure different distances too. The proper length $\kLo$ is the distance between two points measured by an observer at rest relative to both. Time dilation gives the length contraction $\kLrel = \kLo\sqrt{1 - \kv^{2}/\kc^{2}} = \kLo/\gamma$, which shortens the trip to Alpha Centauri for an astronaut with $\gamma = 30.00$. You never notice the effect at everyday speeds, but particle accelerators measure it every day.
objectives: Explain why we don’t notice these effects at everyday scales.
summary_html:
• All observers agree upon relative speed.
  • Distance depends on an observer’s motion. Proper length $\kLo$ is the distance between two points measured by an observer who is at rest relative to both of the points. Earth-bound observers measure proper length when measuring the distance between two points that are stationary relative to the Earth.
  • Length contraction $\kLrel$ is the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer’s frame: $$\kLrel = \kLo\sqrt{1 - \frac{\kv^{2}}{\kc^{2}}} = \frac{\kLo}{\gamma}.$$

figures.original_caption: (a) The Earth-bound observer sees the muon travel 2.01 km between clouds. (b) The muon sees itself travel the same path, but only a distance of 0.627 km. The Earth, air, and clouds are moving relative to the muon in its frame, and all appear to have smaller lengths along the direction of travel.

(a) The Earth-bound observer measures the proper distance between the Earth and the Alpha Centauri. (b) The astronaut observes a length contraction, since the Earth and the Alpha Centauri move relative to her ship. She can travel this shorter distance in a smaller time (her proper time) without exceeding the speed of light.

The electric field lines of a high-velocity charged particle are compressed along the direction of motion by length contraction. This produces a different signal when the particle goes through a coil, an experimentally verified effect of length contraction.

exercises.prompt: A particle is traveling through the Earth’s atmosphere at a speed of $0.750c$. To an Earth-bound observer, the distance it travels is 2.50 km. How far does the particle travel in the particle’s frame of reference?

answer.hint: The Earth-bound observer measures the proper length, so the particle measures the contracted length.

exercises.prompt: To whom does an object seem greater in length, an observer moving with the object or an observer moving relative to the object? Which observer measures the object’s proper length?

answer.solution: The object seems longer to the observer moving with it. That observer is at rest relative to both ends of the object, so he measures its proper length $\kLo$. An observer moving relative to the object measures the contracted length $\kLrel = \kLo/\gamma$, which is shorter, since $\gamma$ is greater than 1 for any relative motion.

exercises.prompt: Relativistic effects such as time dilation and length contraction are present for cars and airplanes. Why do these effects seem strange to us?

answer.solution: The speeds of cars and airplanes are tiny compared with the speed of light, so $\kv^{2}/\kc^{2}$ is extremely small and $\gamma$ differs from 1 only in about the twelfth decimal place. The time dilation and length contraction are real but far too small for us to notice, so everything we experience agrees with the classical expectation that time and length are the same for everyone. The effects seem strange because we never experience speeds where they become large.

exercises.prompt: Suppose an astronaut is moving relative to the Earth at a significant fraction of the speed of light. (a) Does he observe the rate of his clocks to have slowed? (b) What change in the rate of Earth-bound clocks does he see? (c) Does his ship seem to him to shorten? (d) What about the distance between stars that lie on lines parallel to his motion? (e) Do he and an Earth-bound observer agree on his velocity relative to the Earth?

answer.solution: (a) No. His clocks are at rest relative to him, so he measures proper time and they run at their normal rate. (b) The Earth-bound clocks are moving relative to him, so he sees them run slow by the factor $\gamma$. (c) No. His ship is at rest relative to him, so he measures its proper length. (d) The stars are moving relative to him, so the distance between stars that lie along his direction of motion is contracted by $\gamma$. (e) Yes. All observers agree on their relative speed, which is why the distances and times they measure must differ by the same factor.

exercises.prompt: A spaceship, 200 m long as seen on board, moves by the Earth at $0.970c$. What is its length as measured by an Earth-bound observer?

answer.hint: The length measured on board is the proper length; the Earth-bound observer sees the ship moving and measures it contracted.

exercises.prompt: (a) How far does the muon in Example 28.1 travel according to the Earth-bound observer? (b) How far does it travel as viewed by an observer moving with it? Base your calculation on its velocity relative to the Earth and the time it lives (proper time). (c) Verify that these two distances are related through length contraction $\gamma = 3.20$.

parts.part: (a) the distance in the Earth’s frame
parts.hint: Multiply the muon’s speed by the time the Earth-bound observer measures, the dilated time $\gamma\kdto$.

parts.part: (b) the distance in the muon’s frame
parts.hint: Multiply the same speed by the muon’s proper lifetime.

answer.solution:
(a) 1.387 km = 1.39 km
(b) 0.433 km
(c) $\kLrel = \dfrac{\kLo}{\gamma} = \dfrac{1.387\times 10^{3}\;\text{m}}{3.20} = 433.4\;\text{m} = 0.433\;\text{km}$. Thus, the distances in parts (a) and (b) are related when $\gamma = 3.20$.

exercises.prompt: (a) How long does it take the astronaut in Example 28.2 to travel 4.30 ly at $0.99944c$ (as measured by the Earth-bound observer)? (b) How long does it take according to the astronaut? (c) Verify that these two times are related through time dilation with $\gamma = 30.00$ as given.

parts.hint: A light year is the distance light travels in a year, so the time in years is the distance in light years divided by $\kv/\kc$.
The astronaut measures proper time, shorter by the factor $\gamma$.

answer.solution:
(a) 4.303 y (to four digits to show any effect)
(b) 0.1434 y
(c) $\kdt = \gamma\kdto \Rightarrow \gamma = \dfrac{\kdt}{\kdto} = \dfrac{4.303\;\text{y}}{0.1434\;\text{y}} = 30.0$. Thus, the two times are related when $\gamma = 30.00$.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results. (a) Find the value of $\gamma$ for the following situation. An astronaut measures the length of her spaceship to be 25.0 m, while an Earth-bound observer measures it to be 100 m. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumptions are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: The astronaut measures the proper length; divide it by the length the Earth-bound observer measures.
answer.solution:
(a) 0.250
(b) $\gamma$ must be ≥1
(c) The Earth-bound observer must measure a shorter length, so it is unreasonable to assume a longer length.

exercises.prompt: A space rock with a length of 1,000.0 m is moving through space at exactly 0.6 c. (a) If the space rock is moving toward an observer, what is the contracted length observed? (b) If the space rock is moving away from the observer, what is the contracted length observed? (c) Can the object reach the speed of light? (d) If the object were to stop in the observer’s reference frame, would it be observed to have proper length?

parts.hint: The rock’s own length is the proper length, and the contraction depends on the square of the speed.
The speed enters only as its square, so the direction does not matter.
